paragraphs.text: The rays of the light illumine the children of light, and the messages of the light make them radiant. The light of the godly is godliness, which scatters the mist and fog of ignorance. The light of truth dawns on those who love learning: as this visible light gives light to the body, so truth gives light to the soul. By day we tell apart the sick and the healthy, the beautiful and the ugly, the low and the high, the level and the rough, the road and the wrong turning, the thorn and the vine-shoot, the mud and the springs; but by night all visible things [?]. In the same way, brethren, when truth dawns it [?] ignorance and shows the health of faith and the sickness of unbelief, the beauty of humility and the ugliness of dissipation, the baseness of arrogance and the level ground of uprightness, the wilfulness of wickedness, the vine-shoots of virtue and the thorns of sin, the mud of lust and the springs of righteousness.

This is why the blessed David names the light and the truth together in a single strain: "Send out your light and your truth." What light and truth does he want sent? Clearly the light of which John says, "That was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world." For our Lord Jesus Christ is the true light, the ray of godliness, the sun of righteousness, the Dayspring of truth, who dawns from on high and gives light from the earth. From on high, according to his divinity, he dawns in honor; from the earth, according to the economy of the flesh, he rises upward. He is the Dayspring, the spiritual light, which dawns from on high, as the blessed Zechariah, father of John the Forerunner, says: "by which the Dayspring from on high has visited us." The same Dayspring also dawns from the earth, as Zechariah's namesake among the twelve prophets says: "Behold a man, and his name is the Dayspring."

And where does it dawn from? David explains: "Truth has sprung up from the earth." Which truth? Do not learn it from me, but from the Giver of life to all: "I am," he says, "the way and the truth and the life." As was said earlier, in the first discourse, he is a simple and boundless nature, indivisible, incorporeal and without form, as is the Father who begot him. In his beneficence he takes on many different names. He is called the way, to drive out error; the truth, to destroy falsehood; and the life, to undo death.

See how often he takes on names that seem opposed in word but agree in fact. The same one is shepherd and also sheep. "I am," he says, "the good shepherd." And how is he a sheep? John says, "Behold the Lamb of God." Those who want to bring in strange teachings under these different names ask, "How can sheep and shepherd be one nature? Is Christ's nature not divided by these various names?" But it is plain that the various names point not to his essence but to his works. He calls himself shepherd, and is named sheep; he is called priest, and is also named the temple of a priest. Priest, as in "You are a priest after the order of Melchizedek"; and temple, as in "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up."

Let all error be rooted out, and let truth reign as king, holding and ruling over all. Our Lord Jesus Christ named himself the vine, as we went through at the assembly, and he named the Father the vinedresser. In doing so he brought no change of form into the nature; he was telling of the renewal brought by his economy. For everything given to the former people was corrupted. The priesthood was given, and it was defiled; the kingship was given; prophecy was given. Israel became a [?] vine, as the prophet Jeremiah says, and instead of the fruit of godliness it bore injustice. Isaiah says the same: "I waited for grapes, and it brought forth thorns." Since he saw that everything had been corrupted and had grown old through sloth, he came and renewed everything himself. He becomes all things to all, not divided in himself; by a single design he set everything right.

The Scriptures testify that all this had been corrupted and defiled among the Jews: "Their priests," it says, "did not ask, 'Where is the Lord?'" and "their prophets divined for silver," and "their envoys did not know me," and "their rulers dishonored me," and "my people did not know me." Since everything had been corrupted, even the orders of worship, he came in person and raised up the priesthood, re-established the kingship, renewed prophecy, and by his grace restored all that had been corrupted and defiled. The priesthood had been corrupted, so he himself became priest. Of him the apostle says, "We have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." The kingship of the Jews had been taken away, so the King of the saints came in. Of him Nathanael says, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel." False prophecies had hidden prophecy, and God had taken away the grace of prophecy because the inhabitants of the land were unworthy. So he came once more in person to renew prophecy, as the blessed Moses said: "The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you."

So he was prophet, priest and king. He did not need that honor himself; he took it in order to raise up the fallen. The King of kings had no need of kingship. He who received the service of every priesthood was not lacking in priesthood. He who was the fountain of prophecy, and poured streams of righteousness into all the prophets, had no need of prophecy. He took these because he came to raise up all the fallen, and to raise up and renew all that had been corrupted. He also found the vine of Israel corrupted, of which David says, "The vine that you brought out of the land of Egypt: you uprooted the nations and planted it." Renewing what had been corrupted, he says, "I am the true vine." He does not mean that he is by nature something made; he means that by grace he renews what had been corrupted. If the vine is something made, how can he sow like the one who tends the vine? Speaking of his own teaching he says, "Behold, the sower went out to sow," and he explains himself who the sower is: "The one who sows the seed is the Son of Man." How, then, can one and the same be both a thing made and the worker who sows the seed? If you do not distinguish, assigning the one to his divinity and the other to his bodily economy, you confuse the two and will not come to know the truth. "I am the vine," he says, and he calls himself the one who tends the vine, just as elsewhere he is shepherd and sheep. This is how heretics come to read wrongly what was rightly written. As the prophet says, "The ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous will walk in them." They do not understand the right way, nor the refined and discerning judgment of the mind that assigns part to the honor of the divinity and part to his bodily dispensation. So they mixed everything together and corrupted it, and filled the whole world with the mist of error.

For the Savior, the Lord and lover of mankind, came into the world for our sake. He did not leave the honor that he had before the ages; for our sake, in his love for mankind, he set things right. He showed two lights, which together form the portrait of the truth: the divinity through signs, and the humanity through sufferings. For the impassible entered into sufferings through what was passible. He did not take on the passions that lead to sin, but those that belong to the nature we all share. Body and soul are both subject to passions that lead to sin, and whoever is free of those passions is also free of sin. It is like this. Hunger and thirst, toil and sleep are needs of the body and are not counted as sin. But fornication, impurity and debauchery, which defile the beauty of the body, are the passions of sin. The soul too is surrounded by passions of its own, which it received from the Creator by nature as necessary for salvation: fear, sorrow and anger. Taken by themselves they are called passions, but in due measure and season they help our nature.

Take note. There is a righteous anger, a wrath named after righteousness. It does not flare up for nothing; it is the anger of those moved by divine righteousness, very often by the working of the Holy Spirit. It is not when someone grows angry for no reason, but when he is incensed for the sake of godliness. Scripture testifies to this: "The Spirit of the Lord came upon Saul, and he was angered." When righteous anger is put to use for righteous ends, that is praiseworthy. When it is kindled against impiety, when heretics must be silenced, when there is war for the glory of the great King, then showing anger is a virtue and hiding it is treachery. Take note too, brother, of desire: not the kind that falls into sin, but the kind that adorns the generations through lawful marriage. Take note of fear: not the empty kind, but the kind that brings profit and gain. For where there is fear of God there are the gifts of goodness, and where there are the fears of impiety there are empty works. Fear, I say, and the other passions of body and soul that lie outside sin, our Life-giver took upon himself. In the flesh he hungered, thirsted, toiled and slept. In doing so he did no dishonor to the divinity; he did it to show truly the nature of the body. In the same way, in the soul he feared, was troubled and was grieved: "My soul," he says, "is sorrowful even to death"; and again, "he began to be sorrowful and troubled." These were not passions of sin; they made known the nature of the body.

To make it even clearer that such words befit the flesh and not the divinity, the Life-giver explained to his disciples what kind of passions these were: "My soul is sorrowful even to death; stay awake, so that you do not enter into temptation." And immediately he says, "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak." In this way he truly shows in every respect both the honor of the divinity and the economy of the flesh. He ate as a man; he fed others as the lover of mankind. What is more wonderful still, while he was asking for a drink he gives drink to the whole world. To the Samaritan woman he says, "Give me a drink," yet he raises his voice and says, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink." He sleeps on the sea to confirm the nature of the body, and when he rises he puts the waves of the sea to sleep, so that you may learn that he both sleeps and puts to sleep. As God he sees beforehand all that is done in every place, and as a man he went about the regions of Galilee. He came and stood near Bethany, the village of Lazarus, and by the distance between the places he shows himself both far off and near. By the power of his divinity he knows everything beforehand: in Galilee he tells what was being done in Judea. "Lazarus our friend," he says, "has fallen asleep"; he was at work in a place he was not near. He comes and stands at the village and says, "Where have you laid him?" Who will dare to accuse Christ of ignorance because he asked, "Where have you laid him?" If these words cause you to stumble, consider that the Father of Christ spoke words like these too. When the Father says, "Adam, where are you?" is that the voice of ignorance? This voice is the companion of that one. Christ asks, "Where have you laid him?" and in the Old Testament God also asks, "Where is Abel your brother?"

Perhaps someone will say, "That does not solve the mystery; it adds to the perplexity. You have shown that not only Christ asks, but the Father of Christ as well." If that is so, and the sense of the question must be explained for both Father and Son, first learn the meaning of the one who asked there and of the one who asks here. But when I say "his there" and "his here," I do not assign the one to one person and the other to another. What is said in the Gospel I refer to the Father, and what is said in the Old Testament I attribute to the Son. For nothing, whether in the new things or in the old, came about without the power of Christ. John testifies to this about the whole economy and not only about creation: "All things," he says, "came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that has come into being." Now learn the meaning of the question to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" By asking, he opened for him a way to answer. He judges as a righteous judge and calls to repentance as the lover of mankind. "Where is Abel your brother?" he says, bringing him to trial as a judge. Cain took the question to come from ignorance and wanted to hide the deed from his Benefactor: "I do not know," he says; "am I my brother's keeper?" And what then? Consider God's purpose. He who knows all things explains it to him: "I pretended not to know on purpose, and you thought I was asking without knowing. If so, learn the knowledge of the All-knowing: the voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth."

Now learn also the purpose of the Benefactor: in what sense he said to the Jews, "Where have you laid him?" The crowds of [?] were full of contempt. They were a people unable to grasp the wonders of God; or rather, they did understand, and out of contempt wanted to hide the wonders. He saw them swaggering and setting themselves against the wonders. He watched them as they saw the mighty works and denied the one who did good. As David testifies, "In the greatness of your power your enemies lied to you." So what does he do in response? He could have gone quietly. Indeed, even without going in the body, he could have sent his power, and by its rays he could have broken open the tomb, raised the dead man and brought into the light the one shut in darkness. But he wants the scorners themselves as witnesses of the wonders. So before he is shown the tomb, he first draws in many of the scorners: "Where," he says, "have you laid him?" "Come and see," they say, and they show him the tomb. And he says to them, "Roll away this stone." Lord, you gave your disciples your guarantee and granted them power as a pledge: "If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed," you said, "you will say to the mountains, 'Move,' and they will move." You gave them boundless authority; could you not roll away one small stone from the door of a tomb? But, as I said before, the reason is the same: they were unbelieving judges and disobedient spectators. They would have said it was a deception, a trick played before their eyes concerning the dead man, and would have used it as an excuse to [?]. So he brings them to the tomb themselves. When they roll away the stone and the stench strikes their faces, the stench of the dead man will be their witness that he was truly dead. Once they believe that the dead man was really dead, they will not be in doubt about his resurrection either.

Look closely at the order of events right there and you will see that the Lord used these means of condescension. Martha came to the stone and said, “Lord, by now he stinks, for he has been dead four days.” But the Life-giver knew his own power, and his answer was in effect: “That is exactly what I want to hear from you. Say it, and keep saying it, that he stinks. Confirm that he is dead, so that the resurrection may be truly proclaimed.” He spoke of death many times so that the truth of the resurrection would be confessed at least once. After that, brethren, the Life-giver did something else: he looked up to heaven and called on the Father. “Father,” he said, “I thank you that you have heard me.” The disciples of the heretics think they find something to cling to in these words, and they pounce on them at once. “Do you see,” they say, “how great the gap is between them? One entreats and the other is entreated. One pleads and the other listens to the pleading. Do you see that the Father is the source of the miracles and grants the power for them to the Son?” But as I have said many times before, they did not set their minds to discern the works of the Life-giver with gratitude. Once blasphemy had taken hold of them, they were blinded so that they could not discern the truth.

But you, learn the reasons from today’s reading. The Life-giver said to them, “I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of these works are you stoning me?” The Jews said to him, “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, a man, make yourself God and call God your Father.” What grieved the Jews most was that he called God his Father. They were enraged at Christ not only because he broke the Sabbath but because he called God Father and made himself equal to God. Since they counted it blasphemy to call God Father, he held court at the tomb and seated truth as judge. He set those who despised him around as witnesses, so that the very people who said, “You blaspheme, because you call yourself the Son of God,” would see with their own eyes and hear with their own ears. He called on the Father, and by this alone he virtually taught them: “Look, I am calling on him right in front of you. If it angers him that I call him Father, and it is blasphemy as you think, then let him not hear me. But if he is not angry, then it is clear that he truly is my Father.” “Father,” he said, “I thank you that you have heard me.” If his prayers were an act of subordination, how could he say “you have heard me” before he even stood to pray? For before he stood to pray he said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.” And he made those standing around take note: “If the Father is angry that I call him Father, and this is some blasphemy against God as you think, let him not cooperate with a blasphemer. But if I call the dead man and he obeys the command, then take the proof of the truth from the deed itself. For raising the dead is not the work of a blasphemer but the command of the Son of God.” This was the meaning of the prayer. He used it not for any need of his own but for the benefit and correction of his hearers, and he himself testifies to this. When he had said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me,” he added, “I knew that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the people standing around.”

From now on let no one confuse the truth. Let no one insult true religion. Let no one treat the condescension, which was for our salvation, as weakness or as an insult to the Holy One. The lover of humanity became human for your sake. He did not cast off his own nature. Rather, he raises up the fallen and gives life to the dead; he takes what is yours and gives what is his. He did not rise to the highest honor by way of the economy. Rather, he came from the Godhead to take the economy upon himself. It is not as the disciples of the heretics think, that after the cross and the economy he advanced to honor. In their impiety they want to stitch blemishes onto the words of the apostle, who says of the Life-giver: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be seized. He emptied himself and took the form of a servant. He was made in human likeness, and being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.” And Paul goes on: “Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.” “Do you see,” they say, “that he received the honor as a reward for his obedience? Because he humbled himself to the point of death, God therefore exalted him and gave him the name above every name.” If that is so, let them listen. If he was promoted as a reward for the economy, then he went from poverty to riches. Pay attention, I beg you. If he was promoted as a reward for obedience, then he went from poverty to riches, to receive worship from all, so that every knee would bend at the name of Jesus Christ. You say that he was poor and came to riches through the economy. But Paul does not agree with you. He does not show him coming from poverty to riches. He shows him taking poverty upon himself while he was rich.

What does the apostle say? “You know, brethren, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty you might become rich.” He became poor so that you would become rich, not so that you would blaspheme. Our Lord Jesus Christ became poor without casting off his eternal riches, by which I mean the Godhead. He concealed that and took this upon himself. What are his riches? The Father is called rich, and the Son is also called rich: rich from the rich. Paul says of him that God himself makes rich all who call on him, and again, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” In the same way Jesus too is rich, and he became poor for our sake. In what is he rich? He is consubstantial with the Father, the radiance of glory, the exact imprint of his being, and the image of the invisible Father. He did not become so by acquiring it; he showed himself to be so by nature. The riches of Christ are this: he is equal to the Father himself and has the same power, glory and kingdom. He shares the Father’s throne and is honored with the same honor and the same reverence. Yet he who possessed such riches and sat on high with the Father, see what poverty he came down to: he stood before Pilate in court like a man condemned to death. The riches of Christ are the myriads upon myriads of angels who stand ready to serve him. The poverty of Christ is the twelve fishermen who went about following him. The riches of Christ are his throne in heaven and his seat at the Father’s right hand. His poverty is that the foxes had holes and the birds of the sky had places to rest, but the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head. The poverty of Christ is riding on a colt. The riches of Christ are riding on the cherubim, of which the prophet says, “The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold, and thousands are their charioteers.” Have you seen the surpassing riches? Have you seen the poverty that is full of the economy?

But perhaps the heretics have stung you over the loftiness of this theology, and you will say: “Does the saying ‘the chariots of God are ten-thousandfold’ really apply to the Life-giver? Does the testimony you cite have anything to do with him? Did David speak of the Son’s chariots, or of chariots that honor the Only-begotten?” So that true religion is not cheapened in the eyes of sick hearers, and no one thinks the testimony is beside the point, I must show that “the chariots of God are ten-thousandfold, and thousands are their charioteers” does apply to our Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed David says: “The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold, and thousands are their charioteers. The Lord is among them at Sinai, in the holy place. He ascended on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to the sons of men.” That is what David says. Let us call into our midst the interpreter of the prophets, the loud trumpet, the tongue of the Holy Spirit, the man armed with power and every grace: Paul, the singer of the Holy One. Let us see to whom he applies the chariots of God, the ascent on high, the leading of captivity captive and the giving of gifts to the sons of men. The apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all. But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. For it says, ‘He ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and he gave gifts to the sons of men.’” Then Paul puts the meaning of the passage to work and says: “What does ‘he ascended’ mean, except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who ascended into heaven, so that he might fill all things.”

No crowd of tongues is needed to interpret this, and no flood of words to persuade. What is needed is a grateful mind and the unity of faith, united in confessing the Son of God. For Paul did not say “unbegotten and begotten,” or “unmade and made,” because that is not the unity of faith. Listen to Paul, who says, “until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God.” The unity of faith is the knowledge of the Son of God, not of the unbegotten and the begotten. Why do you suppress what is written? Are not the names Father, Son and Holy Spirit more trustworthy than “unbegotten” and “begotten,” and what is written more trustworthy than what is not written?

But the heretic objects: “Then why do you speak of the consubstantial, which is not written?” When war threatens, one must take up weapons that are of no use in peacetime. Who set us among the warriors in this battle, if not hostility from the sea [?]? Or who would get weapons ready against enemies when peace abounds on every side? First remove your “of another substance,” and the “consubstantial” will not confront you. But if you say “of another substance,” the “consubstantial” is bound to collide with you. If you are silent, I am silent too. I recognize that the same substance that belongs to the Father belongs also to the Son. For the names Father and Son carry the same force: the name of the Father and the name of the Son are consubstantial. The Father is the Father of the Son, the Son is the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of God.

But see what the heretics are suffering. They were the first to stir up war, and now they are ashamed to give up that attitude. See how the grace of God responds. It saw that they would not obey the laws of God, so it put them under the force of the laws of the Romans. God always does this. When he sees someone fighting against the laws of true religion, he raises up against them the fear [?] of men, because they did not hold to the fear of God. See what he does: anger is kindled in the mind of the God-fearing emperor, and through God-fearing servants he writes edicts in support of true religion and shoots off his commands like arrows from the bow of the laws.

The Life-giver did the same many times to the Jews who despised him. They rejected his divinity, and when he spoke the truth they asked, “By what authority do you do these things?” He, who was able to bring them to fear men, answered in turn: “I too will ask you one question. The baptism of John, where did it come from? From heaven or from men?” The Jews reasoned among themselves and said, “If we say ‘from heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ And if we say ‘from men,’ we are afraid of the people, in case we are stoned.” Since they did not have the fear of God, they put the fear of men first: “For fear of men we dare not say.” And what did the Life-giver say to that? “Neither will I tell you.” In effect: you do not know at all, but I know, and I am not telling.

In the same way God stirred up the mind of the God-fearing emperor, for kingship is righteousness. Take note: kingship is righteousness when it stands in God’s service. Kingship and righteousness stand on the same rung. When the servants of the kingdom serve in truth, they come to share honor with God. Listen to what Scripture says: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God.” And what does it say of kings? “The king’s heart,” it says, “is in the hand of God.” Why the heart? Because the heart is the spring of the mind and the root of thoughts, and laws come out from that spring, for the words of kings are laws. God holds the heart in his hand so that the laws will not pour out as if from some human mind but will come forth as if from a divine hand. The king lays down laws in harmony with the laws of God. Kingship stands firmly established to avenge the heavenly kingdom. This is not because the kingdom above is unable to take vengeance on its enemies. It is so that the grace of God may open the door of true religion to those who are zealous for it.

If we search carefully, we will find that whenever impiety has gone to war, God has never taken vengeance without some righteous person. If there is no righteous man in between as a mediator, he does not punish the wicked. Instead he makes use of a human instrument full of righteousness. Sodom and Gomorrah acted impiously, yet the five cities were not wiped out until Lot had settled in that land. God did not want the people of the land to say, “There was no one to look to; there was no one whose life we could imitate.” So he brought the righteous man and settled him in Sodom. Lot lived in the same place but stood apart from them in his conduct. So that they could find no excuse in their defense, such as having had no teacher, Lot appeared in Sodom, and then vengeance arrived. They did not imitate either the example or the righteous man, and so they perished in the fiery rain of wrath.

In the same way Pharaoh the Egyptian fought against God, pleading ignorance, and the plagues did not come upon him until Moses had appeared to Israel. Ahab, king of the Israelites, also acted impiously and [?] in lawless impiety, yet there were no threats of wrath anywhere until the zealous Elijah appeared. So too now God is able to take vengeance himself, both his own and that of this Church, which is at war. But he raises up fighters for true religion and wants to care for the Church through the champions [?] of true religion. Likewise blessed Elijah brought accusations against Israel before God when he went into the wilderness, pursued by Jezebel. In response, God said to him, “Why are you here, Elijah?” God asked him, “What are you doing here?” He had gone to the wilderness where Moses received the law, and he said: “I have been very zealous for the Lord God Almighty, because the sons of Israel have forsaken you. They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets. I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.” He said this not as if teaching, but as an accuser. He was not informing someone who did not know; he was bringing a prosecution before a judge: “They have torn down your altars, they have killed your prophets; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.”

Elijah was provoking God as one provokes a judge, and with his accusation he was trying to rouse him to anger as one who punishes. So God wanted to convince the prophet that he spares the impious out of long-suffering, not that he fails to punish out of weakness. He said to him: “Go out tomorrow and stand before me. And look, a strong wind will shatter the mountains and crush the hills, but the Lord will not be in the wind. And look, an earthquake, but the Lord will not be in the earthquake. And look, a fire, but the Lord will not be in the fire.” What does all this mean? “Since you think I am unable to take vengeance, I will convince you that it is not from weakness that I do not punish the sinner. See what instruments of vengeance I have. What the sword, fire and drowning in the sea do for your judges, these things do for me, the great Judge. See what instruments of punishment I have: a strong wind that can not only crush men but also break mountains and grind hills to dust, and the Lord is not in the wind.” As if to say: “I do not want to be known for harshness but to be admired for gentleness.” “Look, a strong wind,” he says, “and it shatters the mountains and crushes the hills, and the Lord is not in the wind.” “Look, a strong wind,” he says, “and it shatters the mountains and crushes the hills, and the Lord is not in the wind.” “Look, an earthquake,” as if to say, “I can destroy with an earthquake too.” “And look, a fire, and the Lord is not in the fire.” He shows these things but does not use them.

You yourselves are witnesses to this. He showed us an earthquake and made fire flash around our city. He frightened us and did not punish us; he showed and then held back. Fire flashed around the city and threats came upon us, but his love for humanity got there first. It was possible, as they say, to see the people fortified and walled in by his love for humanity. It was possible to see everyone finding help from great intercessors, with the kingship and the priesthood standing over them as intercessors. For the God-fearing emperor, joined with our priesthood, interceded and brought God to be entreated. A righteous king can accomplish as much as the priesthood that serves at the altar, and kingship, by its intercession, can win God’s consent. His glory and his upright conduct were displayed through his meekness, and it is clear that he is the son of the great emperor. For the father checked the arrows of the barbarians, and this son by his prayers scattered the arrows that were raining down from the clouds.

Something similar happened in the case of blessed David: God threatens, and then shows his love for humanity. See what the lover of humanity does: “Look, I am setting three plagues before you to choose from. Ask for whichever one you want: famine for three years, war for three months, or death by pestilence for three days.” If you are judging as a judge, why do you give him a choice? Just punish him, for then you would have upheld justice in full. Instead God puts the verdict in David’s hands: “Whatever you want,” he says, “I will do.” Though angry, he promises to comply. But blessed David was at a loss over the choice. “I am hemmed in on every side,” he says, and he does not know what to choose: whether famine would be better, or war, or death. Under constraint he accepts death by pestilence for three days. He does so not at random but so that the king’s godliness may be made plain. “If I ask for famine,” he says in effect, “I will be suspected of caring nothing for the loss of the many because my kingdom has abundant provisions. If I ask for war, I could hand the soldiers over to death and keep myself safe. I will choose death, which passes over everyone alike. It does not defer to the powerful or pity the lowly. It does not honor princes or shrink back from the poor.” He chose this so that it would be clear that he had put himself forward along with everyone else.

“And the angel of the Lord,” it says, “went among them from morning until the sixth hour and killed seventy thousand men of the people.” When God saw that the plague had grown severe and that no one was making entreaty, because the strokes could not be seen, he let David see the angel. The angel held a sword in his hand and hovered in the air. David put himself forward and said, “It is I, the shepherd, who have sinned. What have these sheep done wrong? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house.”

These words are companions to the words he speaks in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd; he lays down his life for his sheep.” When David put himself forward, he moved God to be entreated, and God said to the angel, “Put your sword back into its sheath.” Humility prevailed. It fell down before the great Judge and won his consent. There, the king put himself forward and dispelled the wrath against all. In the same way here, our even more God-fearing emperor clothed himself in humility along with everyone else. Instead of riding in chariots and on horses he went on foot, and by his meekness he softened the punishment. Since he found goodness, he repays his benefactor, and since his kingdom was protected, he works to strengthen the Church. For this very reason God said to Elijah: “Go and anoint for me Elisha as prophet in your place, and Jehu son of Amasiah as king over Israel, and you shall take vengeance on the house of Ahab.” Would a man avenge God? No; God said this to make clear that a God-fearing kingship is the avenger of the truth. So much for that.

From now on, brethren, let us flee from the harm the heretics do and from their endless waves, and bring the ship into the sheltered and peaceful harbor. Let us hurry, before the righteousness of God arrives and sweeps away our sins. Think of wood, grass and reeds lying scattered on the ground in a field. While the weather is calm and clear, they stay where they are, even though they lie scattered. But when a violent flood rises, it carries off wood, grass and reeds all at once. So it will be when the judgment of God comes and the great tribunal of Christ is revealed. It will sweep away all error and cleanse all sins, as the prophet testifies: “Let judgment roll down like water, and righteousness flow mightily like a torrent.”

But here let us bring our discourse to rest and call on our common father, the resounding trumpet, the spiritual instrument. Let us call on what is hidden and what is revealed in the treasures of the Egyptians [?]. It is not for the Church to rise up against itself; its members are to shelter one another. Though they speak many different tongues, the one faith is preached in every tongue. Words do not divide those whom faith does not divide. Speech does not divide those whom the wise men of the Church, in harmony, join to one another. Give voice to every art of the Church! “Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel.” The fountains of Israel are the teachings of the prophets and the law. The fountains of salvation are the apostles and the Gospel of salvation. Come, all of you, and draw the water of joy from the fountains of salvation.
